title: Thirty Spokes, One Hub

zh.text: 三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用。

gloss.3: to share, to join in; some read 拱, “to turn toward, to surround”
gloss.9: not-having: the part that is not there
gloss.11: there is; having (it answers 無 across the comma)

zh.text: 埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用。鑿戶牖以為室，當其無，有室之用。故有之以為利，無之以為用。

gloss.15: to chisel out, to cut through

gloss.32: what is there; having (now a subject, not “there is”)

rendering: is the use of the vessel.
[[Cut doors and windows|hu-you]] to make a [[room|shi]].

thirty.title: Thirty spokes, thirty days
thirty.body: Why thirty? The number was a standard of the craft, and it had a meaning. The Kaogongji, an early manual of the state workshops, lists what each part of a chariot stands for. The square body is like the earth; the round canopy is like heaven; and 輪輻三十，以象日月也, “the wheel has thirty spokes, in the likeness of sun and moon”: the thirty days in which sun and moon meet again. The bronze model chariots found beside the First Emperor’s tomb have thirty-spoke wheels; other excavated wheels have fewer or more. So the first image is also a month. Thirty days go around a center that is no day at all. What is the hub of your month?
src: Zhouli, “Kaogongji”: 輪輻三十，以象日月也。

gong.title: 共: to share, or to bow toward
gong.body: 共 is “together, in common”: thirty spokes have one hub in common. The same character was also used for the word now written 拱 (gǒng): to fold the hands in respect, to surround and face a center. The Analects uses it in a famous line about rule by 德: the ruler is like the North Star, which keeps its place while 眾星共之, “all the stars turn toward it”. Many readers hear that sense here: thirty spokes pay court to one hub. Then the wheel is a small picture of a state, and the center that everything faces is the one part with nothing in it. The Mawangdui silk texts read 同, “same, together”, which supports the plainer sense (see [[their other differences|silk]]). English “share” gives the first meaning and loses the bow.
src: Analects 2.1
Mawangdui Laozi A and B

gu.title: 轂: where the spokes gather
gu.body: The Shuowen defines 轂 as 輻所湊也, “that on which the spokes converge”. The character has 車, cart, at its foot, which marks it as a part of a vehicle. A hub was a short, thick cylinder of hard wood. The wheelwright cut a ring of mortises around its outside for the spokes, and bored a hole through its center for the axle. The hole is the 無 of the line. Without it the wheel is a fine wooden disc that cannot turn on anything. Note the order of work: the hole is not left over. It is bored with as much care as the spokes are cut, to an exact size. The emptiness in this passage is always a made and measured one.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 車部: 轂，輻所湊也。从車㱿聲。

dang.title: 當其無有: where is the comma?
dang.body: 當 means “to be exactly at, to match, to face”. 當其無 is “right at its not-having”: at the very point where the hub has nothing. The refrain comes three times and each time the next word is 有: 無 and 有 touch, with only a pause between them. Where is the pause? The usual reading, which we follow, is 當其無，有車之用: “at its nothing, there is the cart’s use”. Another reading, argued by the Qing scholar Bi Yuan among others, moves the comma: 當其無有，車之用. Here 無有 is one word, “that which has nothing”, as in passage 43, where 無有 enters a place that has no gap. The line then says: “right at its emptiness is the cart’s use”. The sense is nearly the same; the hole still has the credit. We lose only the turn from 無 to 有 across the pause. The Chinese reader sees both cuts at once.

che.title: The cart is a war machine
che.body: 車 can be any wheeled vehicle, but in this period the fine spoked wheel belonged above all to the chariot. States were ranked by chariots: a “state of a thousand chariots” was a middle power, and a “state of ten thousand chariots” a great one. The chariot was the most complex object that a workshop made, and rulers measured their strength by it. So the first image in a passage about nothing comes from the arms industry of the time. A reader at a Warring States court would hear it so: the strength of your army turns on a hole. The Shuowen says the character is a picture, 象形: a vehicle seen from above, with a body between two wheels on one axle.
src: Analects 1.5
Mencius 1A1
Shuowen Jiezi, 車部: 車，輿輪之緫名。夏后時奚仲所造。象形。

shan-zhi.title: 埏埴: hands in wet clay
shan-zhi.body: Both characters have 土, earth, at the left. 埴 is the material: the Shuowen says 黏土也, “sticky earth”, potter’s clay. 埏 (shān here) is the act. The old Heshang Gong commentary glosses the pair: 埏，和也；埴，土也, “埏 is to blend; 埴 is earth”: to work clay with water until it is even. Some editions write 挻, with the hand radical. It is a set phrase of the craft. The Confucian thinker Xunzi uses the same two words for the opposite lesson: 陶人埏埴而為器, “the potter kneads clay and makes a vessel”, and so, he says, goodness is made by effort and is not inborn. Xunzi looks at the potter’s hands. The Laozi looks at the space between them.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 土部: 埴，黏土也。从土直聲。
Heshang Gong commentary on Laozi 11
Xunzi, “Xing e” (性惡)

qi.title: 器: a vessel, a tool, a person
qi.body: 器 is a pot or bowl, and from that any made thing with a function: a tool, a weapon, a ritual bronze. English must choose “vessel” or “utensil” or “instrument”. The Chinese word then goes one step further, to people. A person of ability is a 器. Confucius says 君子不器, “the noble person is not a vessel”: not a specialist with one use. The Laozi plays on the word often: when the uncarved block is split, it becomes vessels (28); the world is a spirit vessel that cannot be handled (29); the great vessel is completed late (41). So the pot in this line is never only a pot. If a person is a vessel, what is the person’s 無?
src: Analects 2.12
Shuowen Jiezi, 㗊部: 器，皿也。象器之口，犬所以守之。

hu-you.title: 戶 and 牖: half a gate, a hole in a wall
hu-you.body: 戶 is a door of one leaf. The Shuowen: 半門曰戶, “half a 門 is called 戶”; look at 門 and you can see the two halves. 牖 is a window in a wall; the Shuowen says 穿壁以木為交窻也, “pierce the wall and set crossed wood in it as a window”. The verb is 鑿, to chisel. Walls were made of rammed earth, and in the loess country of the north whole rooms are still dug out of the hillside. Built or dug, the room becomes a room by removal: you cut openings into solid earth. Door and window return in passage 47: 不出戶，知天下；不窺牖，見天道, “without going out of the door, know the world; without looking out of the window, see heaven’s way”. Confucius asked: who can go out except by the door?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 戶部: 戶，護也。半門曰戶。象形。
Shuowen Jiezi, 片部: 牖，穿壁以木為交窻也。
Analects 6.17

shi.title: 室: the dictionary says “full”
shi.body: 室 is the inner room of a house: a roof, 宀, over 至, “to arrive”. The Shuowen explains it with a pun on a word of like sound: 室，實也, “a room is that which is full, solid”, and adds 至，所止也, “to arrive: the place where one stops”. A room, for the dictionary, is the place that you arrive at and fill with your life. The Laozi line says the opposite thing about the same object: the use of the room is where it has nothing. The two do not contradict each other. A room can be filled because it is empty, and a room packed to the door is a store. Look around the room that you are in now. How much of it is air?
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 宀部: 室，實也。从宀从至。至，所止也。

you.title: 有: to have, not “Being”
you.body: 有 means “to have” and “there is”. Chinese uses one verb for both: “the table has a cup” and “there is a cup on the table” are the same sentence. The Shuowen ties the character to 月, the moon; many modern scholars instead see a hand, 又, that holds a piece of meat. Western philosophy translates 有 and 無 as “Being” and “Non-being”, and the capitals bring in Greek questions about what is ultimately real. The Chinese pair is nearer to the hand: what is there to hold, and what is not. In this passage 有 does two jobs. In the refrain it is “there is”. In the last lines it is a noun, “the having of it”. Passage 2 has already said it: 有無相生, having and not-having give birth to each other.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 有部: 有，不宜有也。《春秋傳》曰：日月有食之。从月又聲。

wu.title: 無: the dancer who became “nothing”
wu.body: The early form of 無 is widely explained as a dancer with long tassels or plumes in each hand; it is the first form of 舞, “to dance”. The character was then borrowed for a word of like sound that means “not have”, and the dancer was given feet (舞) to keep her own word. The Shuowen records the sense simply: 亡也, “to be without”. So 無 is first a verb, the opposite of 有: not-having. It is not “the Void” and not “Nothingness” with a capital, an abyss that Western thought tends to fear. Here it is specific and local: 其無, “its nothing”, the hole of this hub, the hollow of this pot. Each thing has its own. We do not claim that the dancer is in the meaning. But it is good to know she is in the picture.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 亡部: 無，亡也。从亡無聲。

li.title: 利: a blade in the grain
li.body: 利 is 禾, a stalk of grain, beside 刂, a knife. The Shuowen defines it as 銛也, “sharp”, and the common explanation of the picture is a blade that cuts the crop. From “sharp” come the senses “smooth, favorable”, and from the harvest come “gain, profit, advantage”. It was a fighting word. The Mohists made 利, benefit to all, the test of each policy. Mencius opened his book against it: 王何必曰利, “why must Your Majesty say ‘profit’?” The Laozi does not attack the word here. It gives the word a place: the 利 of a thing is in its substance, in that which you can own, count, sell, and tax. Then it asks where [[the other value|yong]] is.
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 刀部: 利，銛也。从刀。和然後利，从和省。
Mencius 1A1
Mozi, “Jian ai”

yong.title: 利 and 用: two words where English blurs
yong.body: The last couplet sets two words against each other, and English has trouble, because “use”, “benefit”, “advantage”, and “utility” run together. 利 is the gain that a thing gives as a possession: the clay has a price, the wall can be measured, the wheel can be bought. 用 is function: the thing at work. The Shuowen defines 用 as 可施行也, “that which can be put into practice”; its early form is disputed. The couplet says that substance gives you a thing to have, and the nothing in it gives you a thing that works. Neither is put down: 以為, “serves as”, is used for both, and 之, “it”, points back at the thing: having it, not having it. 利 is also plain serviceability: wood, clay, and wall give you a thing to work with. Modern life counts 利 very well and has few measures for 用. Legge struggled here; see [[his brackets|legge]]. See also [[Wang Bi’s tighter version|wangbi]].
src: Shuowen Jiezi, 用部: 用，可施行也。从卜从中。衞宏說。

wangbi.title: Wang Bi: gain leans on nothing
wangbi.body: On the hub Wang Bi writes: 轂所以能統三十輻者，無也，以其無能受物之故. “That by which the hub can command thirty spokes is its nothing; it is because its nothing can receive things.” His sentence ends 故能以實統眾, “so it can, by the solid, command the many”; some editors correct 實, “solid”, to 寡, “few”: the few command the many. On the close he writes: 木埴壁之所以成三者，而皆以無為用也。言無者，有之所以為利，皆賴無以為用也。 “Wood, clay, and wall are that from which the three are made, and all three take nothing as their use. What this says of nothing is: that by which having serves as gain leans, in each case, on nothing for its use.” His verb is 賴, to lean on, to depend. For Wang Bi the two halves are not equal: 無 is the root.
src: Wang Bi commentary on Laozi 11

legge.title: Legge’s brackets
legge.body: Legge’s version of this passage is careful and full of brackets, and each bracket shows a place where the English needed help. He adds “(for the axle)” after the empty space, and “(from the walls)” and “(within)” for the room: he explains the pictures and does not trust them alone. In the last line he writes “(positive) existence” for 有, the vocabulary of 19th-century philosophy, and gives 利 as “profitable adaptation” and 用 as “(actual) usefulness”. You can see him try to hold the two words apart with adjectives. For 車 he writes “the wheel”, and so narrows the whole vehicle to one part. His “nave” for the hub is the old English word, and his room is an “apartment”. Read his sentence aloud, then the Chinese count: 有之以為利，無之以為用 is ten characters, five and five.
src: James Legge, The Texts of Taoism, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (1891)

liubai.title: What the arts did with it
liubai.body: This short passage had a long life in the Chinese arts. Ink painters speak of 留白, “to leave white”: the unpainted paper is mist, water, sky, or distance, and it is composed with as much care as the brushwork. Garden builders set a window in a wall to frame a view, so that the window does the work of a painting. Players of the qin, the old zither, give weight to the fading of a note and to the silence after it. In each case the passage’s point holds: the empty part is not a remainder. It is where the work is used. Look at a page of this app. The characters are 有. What lets you read them?

practice.title: Count the nothings
practice.body: For five minutes today, look at made things and find the 無 in each. The cup: its hollow. The key: the cuts in its edge. The flute or the guitar: the bore, the sound hole. The shoe, the pocket, the bag. The doorway that you walk through, which you have never touched. Then widen the view. A week: the day with no meetings. A conversation: the pause in which the other person thinks. Music: the rest. Do not make more emptiness yet. Only notice how much of what you use each day is the part that is not there, and that someone made it with care, to an exact size.

silk.title: The silk texts: a room that is never built
silk.body: The Mawangdui silk texts differ from the received passage in small ways that show how the text moved. They write “thirty” as one character, 卅. They read 同 where we have [[共|gong]]. In the potter’s line they say 有埴器之用, “there is the clay vessel’s use”: the material is named again beside the hollow. In the builder’s line they have no 以為室, “to make a room”: you cut door and window, and right at their nothing is the room’s use. That shorter line is sharper. Door and window are themselves the nothing, and the sentence never builds the room at all. The received text made the three examples match. Which do you prefer: three even verses, or the older, uneven ones? This passage is not among the Guodian bamboo slips.
src: Mawangdui Laozi A and B

pair-you-wu.title: 有 and 無: wall and room
pair-you-wu.body: The passage ends on the pair that passage 2 set first in its list: 有 and 無, having and not-having, here joined to 利 and 用, gain and use. Each example needs both. The hole in the hub is a hole because thirty spokes and a rim stand round it. The hollow of the pot has the shape that the clay gives it. Cut away all of the wall and there is no room; there is weather. So the nothing here is a made nothing. It depends on the something as much as the something depends on it. Readers who love this passage often turn it into praise of emptiness alone. The last couplet does not. It gives [[each side its own work|yong]] with the same two words, 以為. The stress falls on 無 because the eye misses it; people count spokes and clay. The turn is plain in any kitchen: the hollow is for filling, and the full pot is emptied again. Which do you trust more, what you have or the room you keep?

lenses.ground: Three workshops. A wheelwright sets [[thirty spokes|thirty]] into one [[hub|gu]], and the cart works at the hole for the axle. A potter [[kneads clay|shan-zhi]] into a vessel, and the vessel works at its hollow. A builder [[cuts doors and windows|hu-you]] to make a room, and the room works where the wall is absent. After each one the same refrain, 當其無: [[right at its nothing|dang]]. Then a two-line summary: [[having|you]] makes the gain, [[not-having|wu]] makes the use. The examples grow: a thing that carries you, a thing that holds your food, a thing that holds you. The passage has no Dao, no sage, and no advice. You could read it aloud in a workshop as a plain fact, and all three craftsmen would agree with it.
lenses.inner: The fourth vessel is not named: the one who reads. Old practice traditions take the room as the heart-mind and the [[door and windows|hu-you]] as the senses. A mind is of use where it has room. One that is packed with opinions, plans, and commentary on itself is like a pot filled with clay; it has much substance and no place to receive. The passage does not tell you to empty yourself by force. In every example the emptiness is already present and already at work; someone made it with care, and it does not need to be defended. The contemplative step is only to notice it: the gap between two thoughts, the silence in which a sound appears. [[有 and 無|you]] are not enemies here. They make one pot.
lenses.leading: The [[hub|gu]] is the center of the wheel and it does not push the spokes. It holds a place open, and the axle turns in that place. Read [[共|gong]] with its second sense and the picture is a court: thirty face one, and the one is empty at the center. A leader who fills the center with their own voice, will, and presence leaves no room for the axle. [[Wang Bi|wangbi]] says it in a line: the hub commands thirty spokes because its nothing can receive. This is a real kind of influence, and the strategists of the time knew it. But do not turn it into a trick, an absence staged to pull others in. In the passage the emptiness is not a tactic. It is how the wheel is built. The couplet also warns managers who count only [[利|li]]: that which you can measure is half of that which works.
lenses.body: Your body is built like the three examples. The joints work at their gaps: a hip or shoulder turns because the socket has space. The lungs, the mouth, the stomach, the heart’s chambers, the ear canal: each works at its hollow. Stand and let your weight sink. Find the center of the turning, low in the belly. Chinese movement arts treat that place as a hub, and the limbs as spokes. Power that goes through a still, open center is whole. Power from a clenched center breaks at the joints. Then breathe out fully and wait. The pause at the bottom of the breath is 無. You do not make the next breath. It comes into the room that you left for it.
lenses.nature: A valley is land with something missing, and for that reason water, soil, and villages collect there. A nest, a burrow, a hollow tree, a tidal pool, the cells of a honeycomb: living things build with walls and live in the gaps. Soil is fertile when half of it is pore space for air and water; packed soil has the same minerals and grows little. A forest needs its clearings. Time has the same structure: the fallow year, the winter, the night. [[Thirty spokes|thirty]] were read as the days of a month that turn around a still center. The book’s other great hollows are near this passage: the valley spirit (6), the bellows between heaven and earth (5), the empty bowl of passage 4.
lenses.practice: Do the [[five-minute count|practice]] of nothings today. Then choose one container in your life that has become solid: a shelf, a calendar day, a bag, an evening. Do not empty it as a project of self-improvement. Take out one thing and leave the space open for a day. See what the space is used for. In the terms of the last couplet: you already know the [[利|li]] of that which you removed. Find out the [[用|yong]] of the gap. Painters call this [[leaving white|liubai]].

plates.title: The dancer who became “nothing”
plates.lesson: The story of this character is a loan. The early form is widely explained as a person seen from the front, arms out, with a tassel, plume, or branch that hangs from each hand: a dancer in a rite. That character wrote the word “dance”. The word “to not have” sounded nearly the same and had no picture, since you cannot draw a lack. So scribes borrowed the dancer for it. In time the borrowed sense took the character over, and the dance was given a pair of feet at the bottom to make a character for itself: 舞. Set the two side by side, 無 and 舞, and you can see the same upper body. The four dots at the foot of the modern 無 look like 灬, the form of fire in 熱 and 煮, but they are not fire here; they are what the brush made of the lower part of the figure. Other ways to write the word are older in the Laozi itself: the Guodian slips mostly use 亡, “gone”, and the short form 无, now the mainland standard, is already listed in the Shuowen as a 奇字, a variant form of the ancient script. In this passage [[無|wu]] is exact and local: the bore of a hub, the hollow of a pot. A character with twelve strokes, the fullest on the line, says “nothing”. The dance has gone out of it and the dancer is still there.
plates.brush: Twelve strokes, in three bands. The top begins with a short stroke that falls to the left, then two horizontals, then four verticals, then a long horizontal beneath them. Together they make a kind of fence. The discipline is in the spacing: the four verticals stand at even distances, and the gaps between them are as much a part of the character as the ink. The bottom band is four dots, written from left to right. Watch them: each dot leans a different way, the first to the left and the last to the right, with the two in the middle as a bridge, so that the row reads as one movement and holds up the fence. In cursive script the whole character is reduced to a few loops. Zen calligraphers in China and Japan have written this one character alone on a sheet, again and again, for centuries.

plates.title: A chariot seen from above
plates.lesson: Turn the character on its side in your mind. The box in the middle is the body of the vehicle, where the driver stands. The horizontal lines above and below it are the two wheels, seen edge-on. The long vertical through everything is the axle. This is a plan view, drawn as if by a bird, and the Shuowen calls it 象形, a picture. Oracle-bone and bronze forms are richer: many show two round wheels with spokes, the axle, the pole, and the yoke for the horses, and no two are quite alike. The regular script kept the least that is needed. As a part of other characters, 車 marks things that roll: 輪 (wheel), 軸 (axle), 輻 (spoke) and 轂 (hub) from this passage, 載 (to carry), 輕 (light: at first, a light cart), 軍 (army: the Shuowen explains it as chariots in a ring, a camp; the top was at first 勹, “to wrap”), and 庫, a chariot under a roof: an armoury, a store. It is also a piece in Chinese chess, where it moves like the rook. Now read the line again with the picture in view: [[thirty spokes|thirty]] share one [[hub|gu]], and the [[use of the cart|che]] is at the hole. In the character, the stroke for the axle goes through the centre of every other part.
plates.brush: Seven strokes. A horizontal first: the upper wheel. Then the box: left side, then top and right in one stroke with a corner, then two short lines, one inside and one that closes it. Then a longer horizontal: the lower wheel, and the widest line in the character. The seventh stroke is the vertical through the middle, from top to bottom. Watch it. All that is written before it is a stack of level lines with nothing to hold them, and this one stroke joins them and makes them stand; it must be straight and exactly central. The writer makes the axle last, and the wheelwright bores the hub for it with most care. In cursive script the box and its lines became a few quick turns, and that cursive shape was later fixed in print as the short form 车.

plates.title: Four mouths and a dog
plates.lesson: Count the squares: four 口, two above and two below. In the middle is 犬, a dog. The Shuowen reads the scene simply: 象器之口，犬所以守之, “it shows the mouths of vessels, and a dog is that which guards them”. The four mouths are openings of pots or bronzes set out in rows; the bronze forms of the character already have four mouths around an animal. Modern scholars doubt the guard-dog story, and some think the middle was at first a different shape, so hold it as the dictionary’s reading. The square 口 is the busiest part in the script. Alone, a mouth. Three in a stack, 品: goods, grades, to taste. Four, 㗊, the Shuowen’s heading for this very character: many mouths. With 犬 below two mouths, 哭: to wail. 犬 itself is a dog seen from the side, and it has become 大, a person with arms out, plus one dot; as a side part it is written 犭, as in 狗 (dog) and 狐 (fox). The meaning grew from pot to tool to ritual bronze to a person of ability; see [[the note on 器|qi]]. What you see in the character is the lesson of the passage: each of its four corners is an opening. The ink only draws the rims.
plates.brush: Sixteen strokes, in three layers: two mouths, the dog, two mouths. Each 口 takes three strokes: left side, then top and right side together, then the base. Four boxes of one size would be dead, so a good hand makes the upper pair a little smaller and tighter, and lets the lower pair spread to carry the weight. Between them the dog opens out: a long horizontal that reaches past the boxes on both sides, then a stroke that falls to the left and a stroke that falls to the right, like a roof over the lower pair, and its one dot. Watch the white inside the four mouths. In a well-written 器 the four hollows are the same size and shine like windows. The brush makes the walls and the paper makes the [[use|yong]].

questions.claim: A thing works at its empty place; what is there gives gain, and what is not there gives use.
prompts: Do you agree? Find one case in your day where the gap did the work.
How do you count your own worth: by what you have and can show, or by the room you give? Where did that way of counting begin?
Take the opposite for a while: what is there is what counts, and an empty space is a waste that someone should fill. What do you notice as you hold it?
Which do you fill first when you are uneasy: your time, your rooms, or a silence? What is the unease about?

questions.claim: The useful emptiness is a made one: it needs the spokes, the clay, and the wall around it.
prompts: Is that right, in your view? Or is the best emptiness one with nothing round it?
Think of the structures in your life: rules, routines, walls. Did you learn to see them as a cage, or as the thing that makes a room?
Now hold the other side: every wall is a loss of space, and freedom is to have none. Stay with that. What feelings come?
Do you lean toward building walls or toward taking them down? What does each one protect you from?
